questions.question: The entire data-integration argument rests on a single observation. Which?

options.text: No one tool can efficiently serve every possible use case
Distributed transactions are unavailable across heterogeneous systems
An append-only log is cheaper to operate than a database
Batch and stream processing have effectively converged

questions.explanation: Every piece of software, even a so-called general-purpose database, is designed for a particular usage pattern — so applications must compose several tools, and the problem becomes getting data into the right form in all the right places.

questions.question: Why does trying to make one piece of software do everything almost guarantee a poor implementation?

options.text: It is hard enough to get a single code path robust and performing well
Because larger codebases always take proportionally longer to compile
Because no single vendor can afford to hire enough engineers for it
Because one binary cannot be deployed across many machines at once

questions.explanation: 'I want to store some data and look it up again later' has no one right solution, yet any individual implementation still has to pick one particular approach — which is why applications end up composing several tools rather than expecting one to cover everything.

questions.question: All the technical machinery of data systems is in aid of one three-part goal. What is it?

options.text: Reliable, scalable and maintainable applications
A catalogue of every available database product
Impossibility results proved about distributed systems
Fluency in SQL and MapReduce query languages

questions.explanation: The chapter brings all of these ideas together and builds on them to envisage the future.

questions.question: The opening states the goal for future applications using four adjectives. Which?

options.text: Robust, correct, evolvable, and ultimately beneficial to humanity
Fast, cheap, reliable and secure above every other concern
Reliable, scalable, maintainable and fully observable
Robust, correct, performant and commercially profitable

questions.explanation: 'Beneficial to humanity' is unusual for a technical book, and it sets up the closing section on Doing the Right Thing.

questions.question: Across storage, replication, partitioning and transactions, one theme recurs. Which?

options.text: That every problem has several solutions, each with its own trade-offs
That there is always one best solution, which is discovered over time
That performance concerns always dominate every other consideration
That the trade-offs disappear once you reach sufficient scale

questions.explanation: 'I want to store some data and look it up again later' has no one right solution — yet an individual software implementation still has to pick one particular approach, because it's hard enough to get one code path robust and performing well, and trying to do everything in one piece of software almost guarantees that the implementation will be poor.

questions.question: What is true of every piece of software, even a so-called general-purpose database?

options.text: That every piece of software is designed for a particular usage pattern
General-purpose databases serve every usage pattern adequately
General-purpose databases are a marketing fiction with no real referent
General-purpose databases are always the right default choice

questions.explanation: This sentence is load-bearing: it justifies the whole data-integration argument that follows. The first challenge is to figure out the mapping between the software products and the circumstances in which they are a good fit — and vendors are understandably reluctant to tell you about the kinds of workloads for which their software is poorly suited. Another challenge is that you often need to cobble together several different pieces of software.

questions.question: Give the opening example of two tools that must be combined, and why neither suffices alone.

options.text: An OLTP database plus a full-text search index
Integrating two relational databases from different vendors
Integrating a cache with a message broker
Integrating a graph database with a key-value store

questions.explanation: As the number of different representations of the data increases, the integration problem becomes harder: besides the database and search index, there may be analytics systems such as data warehouses or batch and stream processing systems, caches or denormalized versions of objects, machine learning, classification, ranking or recommendation systems, and notifications.

questions.question: Engineers often say 'in my experience, 99% of people only need X'. What does such a statement actually reveal?

options.text: More about the speaker's experience than the technology's usefulness
That the 99% figure is statistically robust across organizations
That the great majority of features are genuinely unnecessary
That the need for data integration arises only rarely in practice

questions.explanation: When the same data is kept in several storage systems you must be very clear about the inputs and outputs: where is data written first, and which representations are derived from which sources?

questions.question: If the application writes directly to both the search index and the database, what goes wrong?

options.text: Conflicting writes may reach each system in a different order
Writes simply become slower, with no correctness problem at all
The search index rejects the writes until the database confirms
The database rejects the writes until the index confirms them

questions.explanation: This is an integrity violation, not a lag — exactly the distinction the chapter draws later between timeliness and integrity. If instead you funnel all user input through a single system that decides an ordering for all writes, it becomes much easier to derive other representations of the data by processing the writes in the same order: this is an application of state machine replication, and whether you use change data capture or an event sourcing log is less important than simply the principle of deciding on a total order.

questions.question: What two properties of event-log-based updates make fault recovery easy?

options.text: Determinism and idempotence
Atomicity and durability
Linearizability and serializability
Ordering and replication

questions.explanation: Updating a derived data system based on an event log can often be made deterministic and idempotent, making it quite easy to recover from faults.

questions.question: How do distributed transactions and log-based derived data achieve similar goals differently?

options.text: Locks for ordering and atomic commit, versus a log and idempotence
Each of them decides ordering with locks and commits atomically
Each of them decides ordering with a log and relies on idempotence
The two achieve entirely unrelated goals and cannot be compared

questions.explanation: The biggest difference is that transaction systems usually provide linearizability, which implies useful guarantees such as reading your own writes, whereas derived data systems are often updated asynchronously and so do not by default offer the same timing guarantees.

questions.question: Distributed transactions deserve a hedged verdict rather than a flat one. Which?

options.text: Useful in limited environments, but XA's fault tolerance is poor
Distributed transactions are always the right answer
Distributed transactions have never worked anywhere
A better protocol already exists and is widely adopted

questions.explanation: Successful in limited environments, poor in general, potentially improvable but not soon. However, he pushes back on the slogan that 'eventual consistency is inevitable — suck it up and learn to deal with it': guarantees such as reading your own writes are useful, and telling application developers to just live without them is not helpful, at least not without good guidance on how to deal with it. The middle ground is developed under Aiming for Correctness.

questions.question: Which limits does total ordering run into as systems scale? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the throughput of events is greater than a single machine can handle, you need to partition across multiple machines — but then the order of events in two different partitions is ambiguous, since constructing a totally ordered log requires all events to pass through a single leader node

If servers are spread across multiple geographically distributed datacenters, you typically have a separate leader in each datacenter, because network delays make synchronous cross-datacenter coordination inefficient — which implies an undefined ordering of events that originate in two different datacenters

When applications are deployed as microservices, a common design choice is to deploy each service and its durable state as an independent unit with no durable state shared between services — so when two events originate in different services, there is no defined order for those events
If more than one producer appends to the same log partition, the append cannot be made atomic, so ordering within that partition is lost

questions.explanation: That last option is false — appends within a partition are ordered. The chapter's fourth genuine limit is client-side state: some applications update state immediately on user input and even continue to work offline, and with such applications clients and servers are very likely to see events in different orders. In formal terms, deciding on a total order of events is known as total order broadcast, which is equivalent to consensus — and most consensus algorithms are designed for situations in which the throughput of a single node is sufficient to process the entire stream of events, so they do not provide a mechanism for multiple nodes to share the work of ordering the events. It is still an open research problem to design consensus algorithms that can scale beyond the throughput of a single node and work well in a geographically distributed setting.

questions.question: When does a missing total order not matter?

options.text: When there is no causal link between the events
Whenever the events are on the same machine
Whenever clocks are synchronized
It always matters, with no exceptions

questions.explanation: However, causal dependencies sometimes arise in more subtle ways.

questions.question: Walk the unfriend-then-complain example.

options.text: Unfriending someone, then complaining about them to remaining friends
Two users concurrently send the same message and one is lost
A user's profile update arrives before their account creation
Two users unfriend each other simultaneously

questions.explanation: The notification is effectively a join between the messages and the friend list, making it an instance of the timing issues discussed for stream joins.

questions.question: Is there a clean answer to capturing causal dependencies, and what partial remedies exist? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The admission: unfortunately, there does not seem to be a simple answer to this problem

Logical timestamps can provide total ordering without coordination, so they may help in cases where total order broadcast is not feasible — but they still require recipients to handle events that are delivered out of order, and they require additional metadata to be passed around

If you can log an event to record the state of the system that the user saw before making a decision, and give that event a unique identifier, then any later events can reference that event identifier in order to record the causal dependency
Synchronizing every machine clock with NTP to within a few milliseconds, which is sufficient to recover the causal order of any two events directly from their timestamps

questions.explanation: The clock-synchronization option is ruled out by Chapter 8. A third genuine starting point the chapter gives: conflict resolution algorithms help with processing events delivered in an unexpected order — useful for maintaining state, but they do not help if actions have external side effects, such as sending a notification to a user. Each starting point comes with a limitation. The subsection ends hopefully but hedged: perhaps, over time, patterns for application development will emerge that allow causal dependencies to be captured efficiently, and derived state to be maintained correctly, without forcing all events to go through the bottleneck of total order broadcast.

questions.question: State the goal of data integration in a single line.

options.text: Making sure data ends up in the right form in all the right places
To store all of an organization's data in a single database
To eliminate derived data in favour of one canonical copy
To ensure every system in the organization is linearizable

questions.explanation: Note that 'training models' sits in the same list as filtering and aggregating — machine learning is treated as just another derivation. The outputs of batch and stream processes are derived datasets such as search indexes, materialized views, recommendations to show to users, and aggregate metrics.

questions.question: What is the main fundamental difference between batch and stream processing, and what about the others?

options.text: That streams are unbounded while batch inputs are of known, finite size
That batch is deterministic and streaming is not; the other differences are permanent
That batch uses HDFS and streaming uses Kafka; nothing else differs
That streaming is always faster; the other differences are cosmetic

questions.explanation: Spark performs stream processing on top of a batch processing engine by breaking the stream into microbatches, whereas Apache Flink performs batch processing on top of a stream processing engine. In principle one type of processing can be emulated on top of the other, although the performance characteristics vary — for example microbatching may perform poorly on hopping or sliding windows.

questions.question: Which functional properties does batch processing have?

options.text: A functional flavour: deterministic, pure, immutable inputs, append-only outputs
Batch processing is inherently stateful and full of side effects
Batch processing requires an actual functional programming language
Batch processing has no functional properties worth speaking of

questions.explanation: The principle of deterministic functions with well-defined inputs and outputs is not only good for fault tolerance, it also simplifies reasoning about the dataflows in an organization: no matter whether the derived data is a search index, a statistical model, or a cache, it helps to think in terms of data pipelines that derive one thing from another, pushing state changes in one system through functional application code and applying the effects to derived systems.

questions.question: Derived data systems could be maintained synchronously. Why is asynchrony preferred?

options.text: Because asynchrony contains a fault locally instead of amplifying it
Synchronous derived-data updates cannot be implemented at all
Because asynchrony is faster and that is the only reason
Because relational databases update indexes asynchronously too

questions.explanation: Fault containment, not speed, is the primary argument. A partitioned system with secondary indexes must either send writes to multiple partitions, if the index is term-partitioned, or send reads to all partitions, if it is document-partitioned — and such cross-partition communication is also most reliable and scalable if the index is maintained asynchronously.

questions.question: Which of batch and stream processing does what when maintaining derived data?

options.text: Streaming gives low delay; batch reprocesses accumulated history
Batch gives the low delay while streaming reprocesses history
Each of the two handles only recently arrived data
Each of the two handles only accumulated historical data

questions.explanation: Without reprocessing, schema evolution is limited to simple changes like adding a new optional field to a record, or adding a new type of record — and this is the case both in a schema-on-write and in a schema-on-read context. With reprocessing it is possible to restructure a dataset into a completely different model in order to better serve new requirements.

questions.question: What does the railway-gauge box concede at the end?

options.text: That conversion is possible but expensive, so nonstandard gauges survive
That gauge conversion turns out to be technically impossible
That all railways successfully converged on a single gauge
That gauge standardization turned out to cost nothing at all

questions.explanation: The moral is not that migration is easy — it is that migration is possible but so expensive that people often don't finish.

questions.question: Describe the gradual migration that derived views enable.

options.text: Maintain both schemas side by side as two derived views
You must switch all users at once after a full rewrite
You must take the system offline for the migration
You must migrate the underlying data destructively

questions.explanation: The beauty of such a gradual migration is that every stage of the process is easily reversible if something goes wrong: you always have a working system to go back to. By reducing the risk of irreversible damage, you can be more confident about going ahead, and thus move faster to improve your system.

questions.question: State the lambda architecture's core idea and its two parallel systems.

options.text: Append immutable events and derive read-optimized views from them
One database and one cache, running alongside each other
Two identical stream processors, run for redundancy
A single unified engine that handles batch and stream alike

questions.explanation: In the lambda approach the stream processor consumes the events and quickly produces an approximate update to the view, while the batch processor later consumes the same set of events and produces a corrected version of the derived view. The reasoning: batch processing is simpler and thus less prone to bugs, while stream processors are thought to be less reliable and harder to make fault-tolerant — and moreover the stream process can use fast approximate algorithms while the batch process uses slower exact algorithms.

questions.question: What does the lambda architecture get right, before its problems are counted?

options.text: That it was influential, popularizing derived views over immutable events
He rejects the architecture outright, crediting it with nothing at all
That it is the final architecture data systems will need
That it removed the need for batch processing altogether

questions.explanation: Influential and directionally right, with practical problems.

questions.question: Which practical problems does the lambda architecture have? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Duplicated logic: having to maintain the same logic to run both in a batch and in a stream processing framework is significant additional effort — and although libraries such as Summingbird provide an abstraction for computations that can be run in either a batch or a streaming context, the operational complexity of debugging, tuning and maintaining two different systems remains

Merging two outputs: since the stream pipeline and the batch pipeline produce separate outputs, they need to be merged in order to respond to user requests. This merge is fairly easy if the computation is a simple aggregation over a tumbling window, but it becomes significantly harder if the view is derived using more complex operations such as joins and sessionization, or if the output is not a time series

Reprocessing cost forces incrementalization: although it is nice to have the ability to reprocess the entire historical dataset, doing so frequently is expensive on large datasets — so the batch pipeline often needs to be set up to process incremental batches, such as an hour's worth of data at the end of every hour, which raises the problems of handling stragglers and handling windows that cross boundaries between batches. Incrementalizing a batch computation adds complexity, making it more akin to the streaming layer, which runs counter to the goal of keeping the batch layer as simple as possible
Joins cannot be expressed in the lambda architecture at all, which is what rules out sessionization and forces every view to be a simple aggregation

questions.explanation: Three objections, all practical rather than conceptual.

questions.question: Which features enable the benefits of lambda without its downsides? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The ability to replay historical events through the same processing engine that handles the stream of recent events — for example log-based message brokers have the ability to replay messages, and some stream processors can read input from a distributed filesystem such as HDFS

Exactly-once semantics for stream processors, so that the output is the same as if no faults had occurred even if faults did in fact occur — which, like with batch processing, requires discarding the partial output of any failed tasks

Tools for windowing by event time, not by processing time, since processing time is meaningless when reprocessing historical events. For example Apache Beam provides an API for expressing such computations, which can then be run using Apache Flink or Google Cloud Dataflow
A second redundant batch layer, run purely in order to correct the output of the first batch layer

questions.explanation: Three features, becoming increasingly widely available.

questions.question: 'At a most abstract level, databases, Hadoop, and operating systems all perform the same functions.' Which?

options.text: They store data, and they let you process and query it
They all provide transactions and a query optimizer
They all provide services over a network interface
They all provide user authentication and authorization

questions.explanation: Of course, there are many practical differences: for example many filesystems do not cope very well with a directory containing 10 million small files, whereas a database containing 10 million small records is completely normal and unremarkable.

questions.question: Match Unix and relational databases to their stated purposes.

options.text: Unix offered a low-level hardware abstraction; databases a high-level one
Unix aimed at a high-level abstraction and databases at low-level hardware
The two aimed at exactly the same level of abstraction
Neither of the two families ever settled on an abstraction worth the name

questions.explanation: Which approach is better? Of course, it depends what you want. Unix is 'simpler' in the sense that it is a fairly thin wrapper around hardware resources; relational databases are 'simpler' in the sense that a short declarative query can draw on a lot of powerful infrastructure — query optimization, indexes, join methods, concurrency control, replication and so on — without the author of the query needing to understand the implementation details. Both are simple, for different people.

questions.question: How long has the Unix/database tension lasted, and how should the NoSQL movement be read?

options.text: Decades, since both emerged in the early 1970s, and still unresolved
The tension was resolved during the 1980s in favour of databases
NoSQL applied the relational philosophy to new data models
The tension is recent, dating only from around 2009

questions.explanation: Fifty years unresolved, with NoSQL as the Unix-side resurgence.

questions.question: Walk what a database does when you run CREATE INDEX.

options.text: It scans a consistent snapshot, sorts the indexed values, and writes the index
It locks the whole table and builds the index in one single pass
It rebuilds the index from the base table on every query
It holds the index in memory and never writes it out to disk

questions.explanation: Notice that this process is remarkably similar to setting up a new follower replica, and also very similar to bootstrapping change data capture in a streaming system. Whenever you run CREATE INDEX the database essentially reprocesses the existing dataset and derives the index as a new view onto the existing data — the existing data may be a snapshot of the state rather than a log of all changes that ever happened, but the two are closely related.

questions.question: State the 'meta-database of everything' claim.

options.text: That the whole organization's dataflow looks like one huge database
That every organization ought to run one single physical database
That databases should be replaced by plain distributed filesystems
That ETL processes become unnecessary at sufficient scale

questions.explanation: Same roles, different machines and teams.

questions.question: Federation and unbundling are two avenues to composing storage systems. What does each unify?

options.text: Federation unifies reads; unbundling unifies writes
Federation unifies the writes and unbundling unifies the reads
Each of the two addresses only the reading of data
Each of the two addresses only the writing of data

questions.explanation: Federation and unbundling are two sides of the same coin: composing a reliable, scalable, and maintainable system out of diverse components. Federated read-only querying requires mapping one data model into another, which takes some thought but is ultimately quite a manageable problem — the author thinks keeping the writes to several storage systems in sync is the harder engineering problem, and so focuses on it.

questions.question: What is the traditional approach to synchronizing writes, and what should replace it?

options.text: Distributed transactions across heterogeneous systems, which he rejects
The traditional approach is event logs, and he proposes distributed transactions
The traditional approach is dual writes, which he endorses
Dataflow was invented precisely because no traditional approach existed

questions.explanation: For example, distributed transactions are used within some stream processors to achieve exactly-once semantics, and this can work quite well — however, when a transaction would need to involve systems written by different groups of people, such as writing data from a stream processor to a distributed key-value store or search index, the lack of a standardized transaction protocol makes integration much harder. An ordered log of events with idempotent consumers is a much simpler abstraction, and thus much more feasible to implement across heterogeneous systems.

questions.question: At which levels does log-based integration's loose coupling manifest? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At a system level: asynchronous event streams make the system as a whole more robust to outages or performance degradation of individual components, because if a consumer runs slow or fails the event log can buffer messages, allowing the producer and any other consumers to continue running unaffected. The faulty consumer can catch up when it is fixed, so it doesn't miss any data, and the fault is contained — whereas the synchronous interaction of distributed transactions tends to escalate local faults into large-scale failures

At a human level: unbundling data systems allows different software components and services to be developed, improved, and maintained independently from each other by different teams. Specialization allows each team to focus on doing one thing well, and event streams provide an interface that is powerful enough to capture fairly strong consistency properties, due to durability and ordering of events, but also general enough to be applicable to almost any kind of data
At a hardware level, by removing the need for any specialized network fabric between the composed components
At a legal level, by shifting liability away from the organization operating the composed system

questions.explanation: System-level fault containment and human-level team independence.

questions.question: State the goal of unbundling, and the decision rule that follows.

options.text: Breadth across workloads, not depth on any single one
The goal is to beat every specialized database on its own benchmark
The goal is to eliminate all databases
The goal is depth, not breadth

questions.explanation: Breadth over depth, in the same vein as the diversity of storage and processing models discussed under comparing Hadoop to distributed databases.

questions.question: What major piece of the unbundled database is still missing?

options.text: A high-level language for composing storage and processing declaratively
A storage engine fast enough to keep every derived view current
A distributed transaction protocol with widespread adoption
Nothing of substance is missing; every necessary piece already exists in some system today

questions.explanation: The second wish concerns caches: it would be nice to precompute and update caches more easily, since a materialized view is essentially a precomputed cache — so it would be interesting to create a cache by declaratively specifying materialized views for complex queries, including recursive queries on graphs and application logic. There is early-stage research in this area, such as differential dataflow, and the author hopes these ideas will find their way into production systems.

questions.question: What is this approach called, and how grand a claim is that?

options.text: 'Database inside-out', from a 2014 conference talk
'Lambda architecture', which he claims as his own invention
'Kappa architecture', a proven production design
The approach has deliberately been left unnamed by its proponents

questions.explanation: These ideas are not his: they are an amalgamation of other people's ideas from which we should learn — in particular dataflow languages such as Oz and Juttle, functional reactive programming languages such as Elm, and logic programming languages such as Bloom. The term unbundling in this context was proposed by Jay Kreps.

questions.question: What can a spreadsheet do that puts it miles ahead of most programming languages for derived data?

options.text: Automatic recalculation whenever any input to a formula changes
Static type checking of the values flowing between cells
Transactional isolation between concurrent cell updates
Distributed execution of a formula across many machines

questions.explanation: Automatic recalculation on input change is the model the chapter wants for derived data.

questions.question: Give the derivation functions for a secondary index and a full-text search index.

options.text: A sort of the indexed field values, versus linguistic processing
Each of the two applies natural language processing to its input
Each of the two is a simple sort with no further processing
Neither of the two qualifies as a derivation function in the sense meant here

questions.explanation: For a machine learning system you can consider the model as being derived from the training data through the application of various feature extraction and statistical analysis functions — and when the model is applied to new input data, the output of the model is derived from the input and the model, and hence indirectly from the training data. A cache often contains an aggregation of data in the form in which it is going to be displayed in a user interface, so populating the cache requires knowledge of what fields are referenced in the UI, and changes in the UI may require updating the definition of how the cache is populated and rebuilding the cache.

questions.question: Which derivation functions are built into databases, and which are not?

options.text: Secondary indexing is built in; feature engineering needs custom code
Every derivation function is built into databases as a core feature
Custom code is needed for all of them, since none is built in
Only machine learning derivation is built into databases

questions.explanation: In theory, databases could be deployment environments for arbitrary application code, like an operating system — however in practice they have turned out to be poorly suited for this purpose, because they don't fit well with the requirements of modern application development such as dependency and package management, version control, rolling upgrades, evolvability, monitoring, metrics, calls to network services, and integration with external systems.

questions.question: Which tools are designed for running application code, and why prefer them over the database?

options.text: Mesos, YARN, Docker and Kubernetes
Only stored procedures, which are preferable
Only PostgreSQL extensions
Databases must run the code themselves, since no such tooling exists

questions.explanation: Specialization beats a database's user-defined-function feature.

questions.question: Functional programmers joke about 'the separation of Church and state' in deployment. What arrangement does that name, and where is the pun?

options.text: Stateless services with state pushed into a database; the pun is on Alonzo Church
Stateful applications with stateless databases; the pun is on Edgar Codd's name
State kept inside the application process; the pun is on Alan Turing's name
Logic pushed into the database as stored procedures; the pun is on Alonzo Church

questions.explanation: In this typical web application model the database acts as a kind of mutable shared variable that can be accessed synchronously over the network: the application can read and update the variable, and the database takes care of making it durable, providing some concurrency control and fault tolerance.

questions.question: What can you not do with a mutable variable, and what did databases inherit?

options.text: You cannot subscribe to changes; you can only poll it
You cannot read a mutable variable; databases inherited that too
You can subscribe freely, and databases support it universally
Mutable variables are notified automatically in most languages

questions.explanation: Polling as the only option is the inherited limitation.

questions.question: What does thinking in terms of dataflow renegotiate?

options.text: The relationship between application code and state management
The relationship between clients and servers over the network
The relationship between data on disk and data in memory
Only the performance characteristics, and nothing conceptual

questions.explanation: Precedents: Chapter 11 discussed treating the log of changes to a database as a stream of events we can subscribe to; message-passing systems such as actors also have this concept of responding to events; and already in the 1980s the tuple spaces model explored expressing distributed computations in terms of processes that observe state changes and react to them. Similar things happen inside a database when a trigger fires due to a data change, or when a secondary index is updated to reflect a change in the table being indexed.

questions.question: Why is maintaining derived data not the same as asynchronous job execution? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Order matters: as we saw in the case of event logs and databases, the order of state changes is often important — if several consumers generate derived state or output event streams, they need to process the events in the same order so that they remain consistent with each other. Many message brokers do not have this property when redelivering unacknowledged messages, and dual writes are also ruled out

Fault tolerance is key: losing just a single message causes the derived dataset to go permanently out of sync with its data source, so both message delivery and derived state updates must be reliable. For example, many actor systems by default maintain actor state and messages in memory, so they are lost if the machine running the actor crashes
Derived data needs exactly-once delivery whereas background jobs need only at-most-once delivery
The two turn out to be the very same problem described in different words

questions.explanation: Note the word 'permanently' — a single lost message is an integrity violation, not a delay. Stable message ordering and fault-tolerant message processing are quite stringent demands, but they are much less expensive and more operationally robust than distributed transactions; and modern stream processors can provide these guarantees at scale while allowing application code to be run as stream operators, doing the arbitrary processing that built-in derivation functions in databases generally don't provide. Like Unix tools, stream operators can be composed to build large systems around dataflow, each taking streams of state changes as input and producing other streams of state changes as output.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of a service-oriented architecture?

options.text: Organizational scalability through loose coupling between teams
Technical performance, gained by running smaller processes
Reduced hardware cost, through denser packing of services
Stronger consistency guarantees between the services

questions.explanation: The advantage is organizational, not technical, and it is conditional on independent deployability. Composing stream operators into dataflow systems has a lot of similar characteristics to the microservices approach — however, the underlying communication mechanism is very different: one-directional, asynchronous message streams rather than synchronous request/response interactions.

questions.question: Give both implementations of the currency conversion example.

options.text: Microservices query a rate service; dataflow subscribes and keeps a local copy
Each of the two queries a remote exchange-rate service per purchase
Each of the two maintains a local database of exchange rates
The dataflow approach polls the rate service far more frequently

questions.explanation: Not only is the dataflow approach faster, but it is also more robust to the failure of another service — the fastest and most reliable network request is no network request at all. Instead of RPC, we now have a stream join between purchase events and exchange rate update events. A footnote concedes that you could avoid the synchronous network request by caching the exchange rate locally — however, in order to keep that cache fresh you would need to periodically poll for updated exchange rates, or subscribe to a stream of changes, which is exactly what happens in the dataflow approach.

questions.question: Why is this join time-dependent, and does either design escape it?

options.text: Because reprocessing later would need the historical exchange rate
Only the dataflow design suffers from the time dependence
Only the microservices design suffers from the time dependence
The time dependence affects neither of the two designs

questions.explanation: Crucially, neither design escapes it. The section ends: subscribing to a stream of changes, rather than querying the current state when needed, brings us closer to a spreadsheet-like model of computation — when some piece of data changes, any derived data that depends on it can swiftly be updated. There are still many open questions, for example around issues like time-dependent joins, but the author believes that building applications around dataflow ideas is a very promising direction to go in.

questions.question: Define the write path and the read path.

options.text: The write path precomputes derived data; the read path serves requests
The write path is the network hop and the read path is the disk seek
The write path is synchronous and the read path is asynchronous by definition
They are the same path traversed in opposite directions

questions.explanation: Figure 12-1 is captioned: in a search index, writes (document updates) meet reads (queries). Taken together, the write path and the read path encompass the whole journey of the data, from the point where it is collected to the point where it is consumed, probably by another human: the write path is the portion that is precomputed, done eagerly as soon as the data comes in regardless of whether anyone has asked to see it, and the read path is the portion that only happens when someone asks for it. If you are familiar with functional programming languages, the write path is similar to eager evaluation and the read path is similar to lazy evaluation.

questions.question: What work do reads and writes each do with a full-text index, and what happens with no index?

options.text: Writes update the index entries; reads search terms and apply Boolean logic
Only the writes do any work, since an index makes reads free
Only the reads do any work, since writes are free with an index
With an index in place, neither of the two paths has work left

questions.explanation: The opposite extreme would be precomputing the search results for all possible queries: then reads would have less to do — no Boolean logic, just find the results for your query and return them — but the write path would be a lot more expensive, since the set of possible search queries that could be asked is infinite, and thus precomputing all possible results would require infinite time and storage space. A footnote sharpens this: the set of distinct search queries with nonempty search results is finite, assuming a finite corpus — however it would be exponential in the number of terms in the corpus, which is still pretty bad news.

questions.question: Describe the intermediate design and its two names.

options.text: Precompute results for the most common queries only
Precomputing all queries, called a materialized view
Precomputing no queries, called a cache
The two extremes are exhaustive, with nothing in between them

questions.explanation: An index is not the only possible boundary between the write path and the read path. Viewed like this, the role of caches, indexes and materialized views is simple: they shift the boundary between the read path and the write path, allowing us to do more work on the write path by precomputing results in order to save effort on the read path.

questions.question: Which earlier system design was really about shifting the boundary between the write path and the read path?

options.text: Twitter's home timeline fan-out
MapReduce log analysis
Shopping cart conflict resolution
The doctors-on-call write skew

questions.explanation: The author finds the idea of a boundary between write and read paths interesting because we can discuss shifting that boundary and explore what that shift means in practical terms. The assumption he then questions: the client/server model — in which clients are largely stateless and servers have the authority over data — is so common that we almost forget that anything else exists; however technology keeps moving on, and he thinks it is important to question the status quo from time to time.

questions.question: What used to be about the only thing you could do offline in a browser, and what changed?

options.text: Scroll up and down in a page you had already loaded
Browsers remained stateless, so nothing about this changed
Browsers gained transactions and an embedded SQL database
Browsers gained server-side rendering of stateful pages

questions.explanation: These changing capabilities have led to renewed interest in offline-first applications that do as much as possible using a local database on the same device, without requiring an internet connection, and sync with remote servers in the background when a network connection is available — since mobile devices often have slow and unreliable cellular internet connections, it's a big advantage for users if their user interface does not have to wait for synchronous network requests, and if apps mostly work offline.

questions.question: When state lives on end-user devices, how are the layers best described?

options.text: Pixels are a view onto model objects, which replicate server state
The screen is the system of record and the datacenter a cache of it
The model objects are the only authoritative state
The layers are independent, so neither is a view onto the other

questions.explanation: Two levels of derivation, from datacenter to device to pixels.

questions.question: Why doesn't a loaded web page notice server-side changes, and what is RSS really?

options.text: Because the browser reads once and never subscribes to updates
Because browsers cannot open TCP connections; RSS is a push protocol
Because servers cannot track clients; RSS is a WebSocket protocol
Browsers do notice changes automatically

questions.explanation: More recent protocols have moved beyond the basic request/response pattern of HTTP: server-sent events (the EventSource API) and WebSockets provide communication channels by which a web browser can keep an open TCP connection to a server, and the server can actively push messages to the browser as long as it remains connected — giving the server an opportunity to actively inform the end-user client about any changes to the state it has stored locally, reducing the staleness of the client-side state.

questions.question: In write-path/read-path terms, what does pushing state changes to devices amount to?

options.text: Extending the write path all the way to the end user
Extending the read path all the way back to the server
Eliminating both of the paths in favour of polling
Replacing the write path with periodic client polling

questions.explanation: Devices will be offline sometimes and unable to receive notifications — but we already solved that problem: consumer offsets let a consumer of a log-based message broker reconnect after failing or becoming disconnected and ensure it doesn't miss any messages that arrived while it was disconnected. The same technique works for individual users, where each device is a small subscriber to a small stream of events.

questions.question: Which client-side toolchains already work this way, and what do they resemble?

options.text: Elm, and Facebook's React, Flux and Redux
Angular and Vue, which use polling
jQuery and Backbone, which use request/response
Client-side toolchains bear no resemblance to event sourcing

questions.explanation: The challenge: the assumption of stateless clients and request/response interactions is very deeply ingrained in our databases, libraries, frameworks and protocols — many datastores support read and write operations where a request returns one response, but much fewer provide an ability to subscribe to changes, that is a request that returns a stream of responses over time. Extending write paths all the way to end users would require fundamentally rethinking the way we build many of these systems, moving away from request/response interaction and toward publish/subscribe dataflow — but the author thinks the advantages of more responsive user interfaces and better offline support would make it worth the effort, and hopes that if you are designing data systems you will keep in mind the option of subscribing to changes, not just querying the current state.

questions.question: What does the store give you that the event log alone doesn't?

options.text: It allows random-access reads without scanning the whole log
The store supplies the ordering that an event log cannot
The store supplies the durability that an event log cannot
The store adds nothing beyond what the log already provides

questions.explanation: Random access without scanning is the store's contribution.

questions.question: What is the proposed treatment of reads?

options.text: Represent reads as events too, and route both through a stream processor
That reads should bypass the log entirely and always will do so
That reads should be batched up and served nightly
That reads should be eliminated in favour of subscriptions

questions.explanation: When both the writes and the reads are represented as events, and routed to the same stream operator in order to be handled, we are in fact performing a stream-table join between the stream of read queries and the database — so the read event needs to be sent to the database partition holding the data, just like batch and stream processors need to copartition inputs on the same key when joining.

questions.question: How do a one-off read and a subscribe differ, seen as joins?

options.text: A one-off read forgets the request; a subscription is a persistent join
Each of the two is a persistent join against future events
Each of the two is a transient join that is then forgotten
Neither of the two is usefully described as a join in the first place

questions.explanation: The chapter calls this correspondence between serving requests and performing joins quite fundamental.

questions.question: What does recording a log of read events buy you?

options.text: Tracking causal dependencies and data provenance
It reduces the storage the event log requires
It speeds up the read path for common queries
The benefits are purely theoretical rather than practical

questions.explanation: Writing read events to durable storage thus enables better tracking of causal dependencies, but it incurs additional storage and I/O cost — optimizing such systems to reduce the overhead is still an open research problem. But if you already log read requests for operational purposes, as a side effect of request processing, it is not such a great change to make the log the source of the requests instead.

questions.question: When is reads-as-events overkill, and what does it open up?

options.text: For single-partition queries, where the machinery is overkill
It is never overkill, and it opens up nothing new
It is always overkill, whatever the partitioning
It is overkill only for multi-partition queries

questions.explanation: Storm's distributed RPC feature supports this usage pattern: it has been used to compute the number of people who have seen a URL on Twitter — the union of the follower sets of everyone who has tweeted that URL — and since the set of Twitter users is partitioned, this computation requires combining results from many partitions.

questions.question: Walk the fraud-prevention example.

options.text: Fraud prevention, joining across several partitioned reputation databases
A single join against one partitioned reputation database suffices
All of the reputation data is held within one partition
Fraud prevention of this kind requires no joins at all

questions.explanation: The internal query execution graphs of MPP databases have similar characteristics. The honest recommendation: if you need to perform this kind of multi-partition join, it is probably simpler to use a database that provides this feature than to implement it using a stream processor — however, treating queries as streams provides an option for implementing large-scale applications that run against the limits of conventional off-the-shelf solutions.

questions.question: Why do stateful systems need more careful thought than stateless ones?

options.text: A stateless service can be fixed and restarted; state remembers forever
Because stateful systems are measurably slower to operate
Because stateful systems are harder to deploy and upgrade
The two kinds of system need equal care in this respect

questions.explanation: Permanent effects demand more care. Transactions have been the tool of choice for four decades for building applications that are reliable and correct — programs whose semantics are well defined and understood, even in the face of various faults. Yet the foundations are weaker than they seem: in some areas transactions are being abandoned entirely and replaced with models that offer better performance and scalability but much messier semantics, as with weak isolation levels and leaderless replication.

questions.question: How good are our engineering methods for judging isolation and replication safety?

options.text: That our understanding and engineering methods are surprisingly flaky
That our methods here are rigorous and well understood
That formal verification has already solved the problem
That the problem is purely theoretical and rarely bites

questions.explanation: Kyle Kingsbury's Jepsen experiments have highlighted the stark discrepancies between some products' claimed safety guarantees and their actual behavior in the presence of network problems and crashes. Even if infrastructure products like databases were free from problems, application code would still need to correctly use the features they provide, which is error-prone if the configuration is hard to understand — as is the case with weak isolation levels, quorum configurations and so on.

questions.question: What are your options, and what do serializability and atomic commit cost?

options.text: Cross your fingers, or pay for serializability and atomic commit
They cost nothing at all and work at any scale
They cost only money, and never architectural freedom
This problem has no established approach as yet, only research

questions.explanation: The author's framing: while the traditional transaction approach is not going away, he also believes it is not the last word in making applications correct and resilient to faults. Transactions are not obsolete and not sufficient.

questions.question: State the thesis of 'The End-to-End Argument for Databases'.

options.text: That strong safety properties do not prevent application bugs
That serializable transactions guarantee application correctness
That immutability alone solves all correctness problems
That application bugs are rare enough to ignore

questions.explanation: The author used this fact to argue in favor of immutable and append-only data, because it is easier to recover from such mistakes if you remove the ability of faulty code to destroy good data — but although immutability is useful, it is not a cure-all by itself.

questions.question: Restate the fork in the road when message processing goes wrong, and define exactly-once.

options.text: Give up and lose the message, or retry and risk processing it twice
Giving up is the only available option, since retrying is forbidden outright
Processing twice is harmless and does not count as corruption
Exactly-once means the message is transmitted only once

questions.explanation: The chapter also calls it effectively-once. One of the most effective approaches is to make the operation idempotent — to ensure that it has the same effect no matter whether it is executed once or multiple times. However, taking an operation that is not naturally idempotent and making it idempotent requires some effort and care: you may need to maintain some additional metadata, such as the set of operation IDs that have updated a value, and ensure fencing when failing over from one node to another.

questions.question: What does TCP use sequence numbers for, and what is the scope limitation?

options.text: To reorder packets and detect loss or duplication within one connection
It holds across every connection between the same two hosts
It holds for the entire lifetime of the application process
TCP performs no duplicate suppression of any kind

questions.explanation: One connection is the entire scope — which is what makes higher-level duplicates possible.

questions.question: In the money-transfer example, what is the failure window and what happens on retry?

options.text: A commit sent but not acknowledged, so the retry transfers $22
TCP duplicate suppression prevents the retry from taking effect
The database detects the duplicate transaction automatically
The retry is harmless because the transaction is idempotent

questions.explanation: The textbook atomicity example is itself not correct at the end-to-end level.

questions.question: Does two-phase commit fix this?

options.text: It lets a coordinator reconnect, but the end-user hop is still unprotected
Yes — two-phase commit fully solves the duplicate problem
Two-phase commit actually makes the problem worse than before
Two-phase commit leaves the connection-to-transaction mapping intact

questions.explanation: For example, if the end-user client is a web browser it probably uses an HTTP POST request to submit an instruction to the server. Perhaps the user is on a weak cellular data connection and succeeds in sending the POST, but the signal becomes too weak before they can receive the response — in which case they will probably be shown an error message and may retry manually. Web browsers warn 'Are you sure you want to submit this form again?' and the user says yes, because they wanted the operation to happen. The Post/Redirect/Get pattern avoids this warning in normal operation, but it doesn't help if the POST request times out — and from the web server's point of view the retry is a separate request, while from the database's point of view it is a separate transaction, so the usual deduplication mechanisms don't help.

questions.question: What does making the operation idempotent through several network hops require?

options.text: Pass a client-generated operation ID through the whole flow
A stronger isolation level configured in the database
A longer TCP timeout on the client's connection
A distributed transaction spanning browser and server

questions.explanation: The example transaction inserts a row into a requests table with a uniqueness constraint on the request_id column: if a transaction attempts to insert an ID that already exists, the INSERT fails and the transaction is aborted, preventing it from taking effect twice. Relational databases can generally maintain a uniqueness constraint correctly even at weak isolation levels, whereas an application-level check-then-insert may fail under nonserializable isolation, as discussed under write skew and phantoms.

questions.question: Besides deduplication, what else does the requests table do?

options.text: A kind of event log, pointing toward event sourcing
It doubles as a cache of the most recent requests
It doubles as a secondary index over the accounts table
It serves no purpose beyond deduplicating the requests

questions.explanation: Deduplication table doubling as an event log.

questions.question: Who articulated the end-to-end argument, when, and what does it say?

options.text: Saltzer, Reed and Clark, in 1984
Lamport in 1978, about ordering of events
Gray in 1981, about transactions
Brewer in 2000, about CAP

questions.explanation: In this example the function in question was duplicate suppression: TCP suppresses duplicate packets at the TCP connection level, and some stream processors provide so-called exactly-once semantics at the message processing level, but that is not enough to prevent a user from submitting a duplicate request if the first one times out. By themselves, TCP, database transactions and stream processors cannot entirely rule out these duplicates — solving the problem requires an end-to-end solution: a transaction identifier that is passed all the way from the end-user client to the database.

questions.question: Apply the end-to-end argument to data integrity and encryption. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Checksums built into Ethernet, TCP and TLS can detect corruption of packets in the network, but they cannot detect corruption due to bugs in the software at the sending and receiving ends of the network connection, or corruption on the disks where the data is stored — so if you want to catch all possible sources of data corruption you also need end-to-end checksums

The password on your home WiFi network protects against people snooping your WiFi traffic, but not against attackers elsewhere on the internet; TLS/SSL between your client and the server protects against network attackers, but not against compromises of the server. Only end-to-end encryption and authentication can protect against all of these things

Although the low-level features — TCP duplicate suppression, Ethernet checksums, WiFi encryption — cannot provide the desired end-to-end features by themselves, they are still useful, since they reduce the probability of problems at the higher levels: for example HTTP requests would often get mangled if we didn't have TCP putting the packets back in the right order
Low-level reliability features are by themselves sufficient for end-to-end correctness, which is exactly why checksums exist at every layer of the stack

questions.explanation: We just need to remember that the low-level reliability features are not by themselves sufficient to ensure end-to-end correctness.

questions.question: Why is the end-to-end situation unsatisfying rather than merely academic?

options.text: Because fault-tolerance mechanisms are hard to get right
Because the end-to-end argument turns out to be wrong
Because the right abstraction already exists but goes unused
Because nobody has seriously tried to solve the problem

questions.explanation: Transactions have long been seen as a good abstraction and he does believe they are useful: they take a wide range of possible issues — concurrent writes, constraint violations, crashes, network interruptions, disk failures — and collapse them down to two possible outcomes, commit or abort, which is a huge simplification of the programming model. But he fears it is not enough: transactions are expensive, especially when they involve heterogeneous storage technologies, and when we refuse to use distributed transactions because they are too expensive, we end up having to reimplement fault-tolerance mechanisms in application code. As numerous examples throughout the book have shown, reasoning about concurrency and partial failure is difficult and counterintuitive, so he suspects that most application-level mechanisms do not work correctly — and the consequence is lost or corrupted data.

questions.question: What kind of abstraction is worth looking for?

options.text: Abstractions giving end-to-end correctness with good performance at scale
Abandoning fault tolerance in favour of very fast recovery
Returning to single-node systems wherever that is possible
Standardizing the whole industry on XA distributed transactions

questions.explanation: Three requirements: easy application-specific end-to-end correctness, good performance, and good operational characteristics at scale.

questions.question: Which constraints need uniqueness, and which others reduce to the same problem? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A username or email address must uniquely identify one user; a file storage service cannot have more than one file with the same name; and two people cannot book the same seat on a flight or in a theater
Ensuring that an account balance never goes negative
Ensuring that you don't sell more items than you have in stock in the warehouse
Ensuring that a user's biography field is never longer than 500 characters of text at all

questions.explanation: A length limit is a purely local validation needing no coordination. A further constraint the chapter does list is ensuring that a meeting room does not have overlapping bookings. Techniques that enforce uniqueness can often be used for these kinds of constraints as well.

questions.question: Why does a uniqueness constraint require consensus, and how is the check scaled out?

options.text: Because the system must decide which of the concurrent requests wins
Because uniqueness requires linearizability, which cannot be partitioned
Because uniqueness requires a distributed transaction across all partitions
Uniqueness does not require consensus

questions.explanation: However, asynchronous multi-leader replication is ruled out, because it could happen that different leaders concurrently accept conflicting writes, and thus the values are no longer unique. If you want to be able to immediately reject any writes that would violate the constraint, synchronous coordination is unavoidable.

questions.question: What guarantee does the log provide, and what makes the decision unambiguous?

options.text: Total order broadcast, plus single-threaded sequential consumption
The log provides at-least-once delivery; a distributed lock makes the decision
The log provides durability only; clocks make the decision
The log provides nothing relevant to uniqueness

questions.explanation: Total order plus single-threaded sequential consumption gives a deterministic winner.

questions.question: Give the three steps of the log-based username uniqueness algorithm. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Every request for a username is encoded as a message, and appended to a partition determined by the hash of the username

A stream processor sequentially reads the requests in the log, using a local database to keep track of which usernames are taken: for every request for a username that is available it records the name as taken and emits a success message to an output stream, and for every request for a username that is already taken it emits a rejection message to an output stream
The client that requested the username watches the output stream and waits for a success or rejection message corresponding to its request
The client polls a global lock service to check the name before it appends anything to the log

questions.explanation: The algorithm is basically the same as implementing linearizable storage using total order broadcast, and it scales easily to a large request throughput by increasing the number of partitions, as each partition can be processed independently. The approach works not only for uniqueness constraints but also for many other kinds of constraints: its fundamental principle is that any writes that may conflict are routed to the same partition and processed sequentially. The definition of a conflict may depend on the application, but the stream processor can use arbitrary logic to validate a request — an idea similar to the approach pioneered by Bayou in the 1990s.

questions.question: In the money-transfer example, which partitions are involved and what does the traditional approach cost?

options.text: Three: the request ID, the payer account, and the payee account
Only one partition is involved, so there is no cost
Two partitions are involved and coordination is free
Four partitions are involved and no coordination is needed

questions.explanation: Independent data forced into a shared total order is what costs throughput.

questions.question: Give the three steps of the multi-partition transfer without atomic commit. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The request to transfer money from account A to account B is given a unique request ID by the client, and appended to a log partition based on the request ID

A stream processor reads the log of requests; for each request message it emits two messages to output streams — a debit instruction to the payer account A, partitioned by A, and a credit instruction to the payee account B, partitioned by B — with the original request ID included in those emitted messages
Further processors consume the streams of credit and debit instructions, deduplicate by request ID, and apply the changes to the account balances
A coordinator performs a two-phase commit across all three of the partitions that are involved

questions.explanation: Steps 1 and 2 are necessary because if the client directly sent the credit and debit instructions, it would require an atomic commit across those two partitions to ensure that either both or neither happen. To avoid the need for a distributed transaction we first durably log the request as a single message, and then derive the credit and debit instructions from that first message — single-object writes are atomic in almost all data systems, so the request either appears in the log or it doesn't, without any need for a multi-partition atomic commit.

questions.question: The stream processor in step 2 crashes. Why is the resulting duplication harmless?

options.text: Because it is deterministic, so duplicates can be deduplicated downstream
Because the crash discards the duplicate instructions as it restarts
Because the checkpoint prevents any reprocessing from happening
The duplication is harmful, and the money ends up transferred twice

questions.explanation: Determinism plus end-to-end request IDs make the duplicates absorbable. If you want to ensure that the payer account is not overdrawn by this transfer, you can additionally have a stream processor, partitioned by payer account number, that maintains account balances and validates transactions — only valid transactions would then be placed in the request log in step 1. By breaking down the multi-partition transaction into two differently partitioned stages and using the end-to-end request ID, we have achieved the same correctness property — every request is applied exactly once to both the payer and payee accounts — even in the presence of faults, and without using an atomic commit protocol.

questions.question: What convenient property do transactions have that unbundled stages don't?

options.text: Linearizability, so a writer's committed writes are immediately visible
Transactions are asynchronous while unbundled stages are synchronous
Each of the two is linearizable in the same sense
Linearizability is offered by neither of the two arrangements

questions.explanation: Crucially, the correctness of the uniqueness check does not depend on whether the sender of the message waits for the outcome: the waiting only has the purpose of synchronously informing the sender whether or not the uniqueness check succeeded, but this notification can be decoupled from the effects of processing the message.

questions.question: 'Consistency' conflates timeliness and integrity. What does each of the two actually mean?

options.text: Timeliness is being up to date; integrity is absence of corruption
Timeliness means absence of corruption and integrity means up-to-dateness
The two words mean the same thing in different contexts
Timeliness concerns durability and integrity concerns availability

questions.explanation: The CAP theorem uses consistency in the sense of linearizability, which is a strong way of achieving timeliness — weaker timeliness properties like read-after-write consistency can also be useful. If integrity is violated, the inconsistency is permanent: waiting and trying again is not going to fix database corruption in most cases; instead explicit checking and repair is needed. In the context of ACID transactions, consistency is usually understood as some kind of application-specific notion of integrity, with atomicity and durability as important tools for preserving it.

questions.question: State the distinction between timeliness and integrity in slogan form, and which matters more.

options.text: Eventual consistency versus perpetual inconsistency
Violations of integrity are eventual and violations of timeliness perpetual; timeliness matters more
Both kinds of violation are equally serious
Both kinds of violation matter equally little in practice

questions.explanation: On a credit card statement it is not surprising if a transaction made within the last 24 hours does not yet appear — we know banks reconcile and settle transactions asynchronously, and timeliness is not very important here. But it would be very bad if the statement balance was not equal to the sum of the transactions plus the previous statement balance, an error in the sums, or if a transaction was charged to you but not paid to the merchant, disappearing money — such problems would be violations of the integrity of the system.

questions.question: Why is the timeliness/integrity distinction inconsequential under ACID, and what do dataflow systems do?

options.text: Because ACID provides both at once, so the distinction rarely surfaces
Because ACID transactions provide neither of the two properties
Because dataflow systems always provide both of them at once
Because the distinction is inconsequential in every system

questions.explanation: Exactly-once or effectively-once semantics is a mechanism for preserving integrity: if an event is lost, or if an event takes effect twice, the integrity of a data system could be violated — so fault-tolerant message delivery and duplicate suppression, for example idempotent operations, are important for maintaining the integrity of a data system in the face of faults.

questions.question: Which mechanisms achieve integrity without atomic commit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Representing the content of the write operation as a single message, which can easily be written atomically — an approach that fits very well with event sourcing
Deriving all other state updates from that single message using deterministic derivation functions, similar to stored procedures
Passing a client-generated request ID through all these levels of processing, enabling end-to-end duplicate suppression and idempotence
Holding a distributed lock across every affected partition for the entire duration of the write

questions.explanation: A cross-partition lock is exactly the coordination the chapter is avoiding. The fourth mechanism it actually lists is making messages immutable and allowing derived data to be reprocessed from time to time, which makes it easier to recover from bugs. Reliable stream processing systems can preserve integrity without requiring distributed transactions and an atomic commit protocol, which means they can potentially achieve comparable correctness with much better performance and operational robustness. This combination of mechanisms seems to the author a very promising direction for building fault-tolerant applications in the future.

questions.question: Which limitation is unavoidable for a traditional uniqueness constraint, and what follows from it?

options.text: That a traditional uniqueness constraint unavoidably requires consensus
That uniqueness is simply impossible in a distributed system
That consensus can be avoided altogether for uniqueness
That every application needs strict uniqueness guarantees

questions.explanation: If two people concurrently register the same username or book the same seat, you can send one of them a message to apologize and ask them to choose a different one — this kind of change to correct a mistake is called a compensating transaction.

questions.question: Reconstruct the forklift-truck argument.

options.text: Order more stock and apologize, as you would after a forklift accident
Warehouse stock must be linearizable because physical goods are involved
Forklift accidents prove that constraints must be enforced synchronously
Apologies are never acceptable in commerce

questions.explanation: The physical world already forces you to have an apology workflow, so the constraint need not be linearizable. Many airlines overbook airplanes in the expectation that some passengers will miss their flight, and many hotels overbook rooms expecting that some guests will cancel — in these cases the constraint of 'one person per seat' is deliberately violated for business reasons, and compensation processes such as refunds, upgrades, or a complimentary room at a neighboring hotel are put in place. Even if there was no overbooking, apology and compensation processes would be needed in order to deal with flights being cancelled due to bad weather or staff on strike.

questions.question: Give the bank overdraft example, and say how expensive apologies typically are.

options.text: Charge an overdraft fee and ask for the money back
That apologies are always prohibitively expensive to make
That banks never permit an account to become overdrawn
That the cost of an apology is effectively always zero

questions.explanation: Whether the cost of the apology is acceptable is a business decision — and if it is acceptable, the traditional model of checking all constraints before even writing the data is unnecessarily restrictive, and a linearizable constraint is not needed. It may well be a reasonable choice to go ahead with a write optimistically and to check the constraint after the fact; you can still ensure that the validation occurs before doing things that would be expensive to recover from, but that doesn't imply you must do the validation before you even write the data.

questions.question: Which of the two properties do these loosely-constrained applications need?

options.text: Integrity, but not timeliness of the constraint check
They require timeliness of the check but not integrity
They require both of the two properties equally
They require neither of the two properties at all

questions.explanation: Integrity without timeliness is the sweet spot for these applications.

questions.question: Give both observations behind coordination avoidance.

options.text: Dataflow keeps integrity without coordination, and loose constraints suffice
Dataflow systems require atomic commit, and applications need strict constraints
Dataflow systems cannot maintain integrity, but applications don't need it
Coordination is unavoidable, and every constraint must be checked synchronously

questions.explanation: Such coordination-avoiding data systems have a lot of appeal: they can achieve better performance and fault tolerance than systems that need to perform synchronous coordination. For example, such a system could operate distributed across multiple datacenters in a multi-leader configuration, asynchronously replicating between regions — any one datacenter can continue operating independently from the others, because no synchronous cross-region coordination is required. Such a system would have weak timeliness guarantees, since it could not be linearizable without introducing coordination, but it can still have strong integrity guarantees. In this context serializable transactions are still useful as part of maintaining derived state, but they can be run at a small scope where they work well; heterogeneous distributed transactions such as XA transactions are not required, and synchronous coordination can still be introduced in places where it is needed.

questions.question: There is another way of looking at coordination and constraints. What is it?

options.text: That they trade apologies for inconsistency against apologies for downtime
That coordination removes the need for apologies altogether
That apologies and coordination are unrelated concerns with no trade-off between them
That availability problems never themselves give rise to apologies

questions.explanation: Two sources of apology, traded against each other.

questions.question: What is a system model, and what is wrong with treating faults as binary?

options.text: The assumptions we make about what can and cannot go wrong
A system model is a performance model; the binary framing is exactly right
A system model is a deployment topology; faults are strictly binary
System models are not used in practice

questions.explanation: We have seen that data can become corrupted while it is sitting untouched on disks, and that data corruption on the network can sometimes evade the TCP checksums — maybe this is something we should be paying more attention to?

questions.question: What first-hand evidence shows that random memory corruption really happens, and with what caveat?

options.text: Crash reports explicable only by random bit-flips in device memory
Bit flips are common and should be assumed to happen constantly
Bit flips cannot occur at all on modern ECC-equipped hardware
Field evidence for this is limited to laboratory experiments only

questions.explanation: Rare but not impossible, and therefore deserving of attention.

questions.question: Which two bugs in mature, widely used relational databases show that even battle-tested code loses data?
