options.text: MySQL mismaintaining a uniqueness constraint, and PostgreSQL write skew
Oracle losing committed transactions, and SQL Server deadlocking
Mature databases have proved free of integrity bugs of this kind
Only bugs in immature NoSQL databases, never mature ones

questions.explanation: When it comes to application code we have to assume many more bugs, since most applications don't receive anywhere near the amount of review and testing that database code does — and many applications don't even correctly use the features that databases offer for preserving integrity, such as foreign key or uniqueness constraints. Consistency in the sense of ACID is based on the idea that the database starts off in a consistent state and a transaction transforms it from one consistent state to another, so we expect the database to always be in a consistent state; however this notion only makes sense if you assume that the transaction is free from bugs — if the application uses the database incorrectly in some way, for example using a weak isolation level unsafely, the integrity of the database cannot be guaranteed.

questions.question: Define auditing, and is it only a concern for financial applications?

options.text: Auditing — checking the integrity of the data
Auditing is only relevant to financial applications
Auditing means logging all queries
Auditing is unnecessary if you use ACID transactions

questions.explanation: Large-scale storage systems such as HDFS and Amazon S3 do not fully trust disks: they run background processes that continually read back files, compare them to other replicas, and move files from one disk to another, in order to mitigate the risk of silent corruption. Two lessons follow: if you want to be sure that your data is still there, you have to actually read it and check — most of the time it will still be there, but if it isn't you really want to find out sooner rather than later; and by the same argument, it is important to try restoring from your backups from time to time, otherwise you may only find out that your backup is broken when it is too late and you have already lost data. Don't just blindly trust that it is all working.

questions.question: What do HDFS and S3 still assume, and what would be better?

options.text: That disks work correctly most of the time, not always
They assume disks always work correctly, and he agrees
They assume disks never work, and he wants more trust
They make no assumptions about disks

questions.explanation: The author fears that the culture of ACID databases has led us toward developing applications on the basis of blindly trusting technology, such as a transaction mechanism, and neglecting any sort of auditability in the process: since the technology we trusted worked well enough most of the time, auditing mechanisms were not deemed worth the investment. But then the database landscape changed — weaker consistency guarantees became the norm under the banner of NoSQL, and less mature storage technologies became widely used — yet because the audit mechanisms had not been developed, we continued building applications on the basis of blind trust, even though this approach had now become more dangerous.

questions.question: Why are transactions hard to audit, and why is event sourcing better?

options.text: Because the transaction's intent cannot be recovered from the mutations
Transactions audit easily, whereas event sourcing audits poorly
Auditing is unsupported by either of the two approaches
The two approaches support auditing equally well

questions.explanation: Being explicit about dataflow makes the provenance of data much clearer, which makes integrity checking much more feasible: for the event log we can use hashes to check that the event storage has not been corrupted, and for any derived state we can rerun the batch and stream processors that derived it from the event log in order to check whether we get the same result, or even run a redundant derivation in parallel. A deterministic and well-defined dataflow also makes it easier to debug and trace the execution of a system in order to determine why it did something — if something unexpected occurred, it is valuable to have the diagnostic capability to reproduce the exact circumstances that led to the unexpected event, a kind of time-travel debugging capability.

questions.question: Why should integrity checks be end-to-end?

options.text: Because no individual component can be fully trusted
Because per-component checks are sufficient and cheaper
Because end-to-end checks are required by law
Because integrity checks are unnecessary

questions.explanation: Implicit coverage of every component along the path is the payoff.

questions.question: What do applications do today about auditing, and what are cryptocurrencies from a data-systems view?

options.text: Few make it a top-level concern; some log changes to an audit table
All data systems make auditability a top-level concern
Cryptocurrencies are purely financial instruments with no data-systems content
Signing the log guarantees the right transactions went in

questions.explanation: The author is somewhat skeptical about the Byzantine fault tolerance aspects of these technologies, and finds the technique of proof of work — Bitcoin mining — extraordinarily wasteful; the transaction throughput of Bitcoin is rather low, albeit for political and economic reasons more than technical ones. However, the integrity checking aspects are interesting. Cryptographic auditing and integrity checking often relies on Merkle trees, which are trees of hashes that can be used to efficiently prove that a record appears in some dataset. Outside of the hype of cryptocurrencies, certificate transparency is a security technology that relies on Merkle trees to check the validity of TLS/SSL certificates — and he could imagine integrity-checking and auditing algorithms, like those of certificate transparency and distributed ledgers, becoming more widely used in data systems in general.

questions.question: An ethical treatment of data systems has to begin somewhere. Where?

options.text: With the purpose every system is built for: the people it affects
With an inventory of the available technical building blocks
With the open research topics that remain unsolved in the field
With product recommendations for each kind of use case

questions.explanation: We talk about data as an abstract thing, but remember that many datasets are about people: their behavior, their interests, their identity. We must treat such data with humanity and respect. Users are humans too, and human dignity is paramount.

questions.question: Which ethical guideline exists for software engineers, and how much force does it have?

options.text: The ACM's Software Engineering Code of Ethics and Professional Practice
The IEEE code of ethics, which is widely enforced in practice
Professional guidelines of this kind have never been written
The GDPR, which functions as the industry's code of ethics

questions.explanation: A technology is not good or bad in itself — what matters is how it is used and how it affects people. This is true for a software system like a search engine in much the same way as it is for a weapon like a gun. But the author thinks it is not sufficient for software engineers to focus exclusively on the technology and ignore its consequences: the ethical responsibility is ours to bear also. Reasoning about ethics is difficult, but it is too important to ignore.

questions.question: Which distinction matters within predictive analytics?

options.text: Predicting weather, versus predicting whether a convict will reoffend
Between supervised and unsupervised learning methods
Between batch prediction and streaming prediction
Predictive analytics is treated as a single undivided category

questions.explanation: Naturally, payment networks want to prevent fraudulent transactions, banks want to avoid bad loans, airlines want to avoid hijackings, and companies want to avoid hiring ineffective or untrustworthy people. From their point of view the cost of a missed business opportunity is low, but the cost of a bad loan or a problematic employee is much higher, so it is natural for organizations to want to be cautious — if in doubt, they are better off saying no.

questions.question: What is an 'algorithmic prison', and how does it invert the presumption of innocence?

options.text: Systematic exclusion from jobs, travel, insurance and finance
It refers to the literal imprisonment of software engineers
It refers to the computational complexity limits of the algorithm
It is a metaphor for lock contention in a database

questions.explanation: Note the parenthetical 'accurately or falsely' — the harm does not depend on the label being wrong.

questions.question: What extra step does predictive analytics take beyond automating a human decision?

options.text: The rules themselves are inferred from data, and are opaque
It makes the decision rules explicit and auditable
It removes the bias present in the input data
It takes no step beyond automating the human decision

questions.explanation: In many countries anti-discrimination laws prohibit treating people differently depending on protected traits such as ethnicity, age, gender, sexuality, disability or beliefs. Other features of a person's data may be analyzed — but what happens if they are correlated with protected traits? For example, in racially segregated neighborhoods a person's postal code or even their IP address is a strong predictor of race. Put like this, it seems ridiculous to believe that an algorithm could somehow take biased data as input and produce fair and impartial output from it — yet this belief often seems to be implied by proponents of data-driven decision making, an attitude that has been satirized as 'machine learning is like money laundering for bias'.

questions.question: What do predictive analytics systems do to the past, and what is the closing slogan?

options.text: They extrapolate the past, so a discriminatory past gets codified
They correct historical bias automatically, so data should lead
They ignore the past entirely and model only the present
They predict the future without reference to any data

questions.explanation: 'Data and models should be our tools, not our masters' is the closing line of the subsection.

questions.question: Which questions arise about responsibility and accountability for algorithms? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If a human makes a mistake they can be held accountable, and the person affected by the decision can appeal. Algorithms make mistakes too, but who is accountable if they go wrong?
When a self-driving car causes an accident, who is responsible?
If an automated credit scoring algorithm systematically discriminates against people of a particular race or religion, is there any recourse?
If you publish your model's source code, does that automatically discharge your accountability for it?

questions.explanation: Publishing source code is not one of the chapter's questions; a fourth that is: if a decision by your machine learning system comes under judicial review, can you explain to the judge how the algorithm made its decision? The chapter claims to answer none of them.

questions.question: Why are credit rating agencies the 'old example', and how do machine learning scores differ?

options.text: A credit score rests on relevant facts and errors can be corrected
Credit scores are opaque while machine learning scores are transparent
Credit scores cannot be corrected while ML scores can be
The two kinds of score differ in no material respect at all

questions.explanation: The two properties a credit score has are relevance of the inputs and correctability of errors. A credit score summarizes 'How did you behave in the past?' whereas predictive analytics usually work on the basis of 'Who is similar to you, and how did people like you behave in the past?' Drawing parallels to others' behavior implies stereotyping people, for example based on where they live — a close proxy for race and socioeconomic class. What about people who get put in the wrong bucket? Furthermore, if a decision is incorrect due to erroneous data, recourse is almost impossible.

questions.question: Walk the life-expectancy argument.

options.text: That a correct distribution says little about any individual case
Averages apply exactly to individuals, so predictions are reliable
Probability distributions guarantee individual accuracy
Statistical data cannot be used for prediction at all

questions.explanation: A blind belief in the supremacy of data for making decisions is not only delusional, it is positively dangerous. As data-driven decision making becomes more widespread, we will need to figure out how to make algorithms accountable and transparent, how to avoid reinforcing existing biases, and how to fix them when they inevitably make mistakes.

questions.question: Give an example of analytics that cuts both ways.

options.text: It can direct aid, or help predatory businesses find the vulnerable
Analytics of this kind can only ever be used for good
Analytics of this kind can only ever be used for harm
It applies only to aggregate populations, never to individuals

questions.explanation: Even with predictive applications that have less immediately far-reaching effects on people, such as recommendation systems, there are difficult issues: when services become good at predicting what content users want to see, they may end up showing people only opinions they already agree with, leading to echo chambers in which stereotypes, misinformation and polarization can breed — and we are already seeing the impact of social media echo chambers on election campaigns.

questions.question: Trace the credit-score employment feedback loop.

options.text: Missed payments lower the score, which then costs you the job
Credit scores improve employment prospects in a virtuous cycle
Employers do not in practice consult credit scores at all
The feedback loop corrects itself once employment resumes

questions.explanation: When predictive analytics affect people's lives, particularly pernicious problems arise due to self-reinforcing feedback loops. We can't always predict when such feedback loops happen — however, many consequences can be predicted by thinking about the entire system, not just the computerized parts but also the people interacting with it, an approach known as systems thinking. We can try to understand how a data analysis system responds to different behaviors, structures or characteristics: does the system reinforce and amplify existing differences between people, for example making the rich richer or the poor poorer, or does it try to combat injustice? And even with the best intentions, we must beware of unintended consequences.

questions.question: Two kinds of data collection stand in different relationships to the user. Distinguish them.

options.text: Explicit entry serves the user; side-effect tracking serves other interests
The two relationships are identical in kind and in effect
Side-effect tracking always serves the user's own interest
Explicit entry always works against the user's own interest

questions.explanation: Tracking behavioral data has become increasingly important for user-facing features of many online services: tracking which search results are clicked helps improve the ranking of search results; recommending 'people who liked X also liked Y' helps users discover interesting and useful things; and A/B tests and user flow analysis can help indicate how a user interface might be improved. Those features require some amount of tracking of user behavior, and users benefit from them.

questions.question: What does the advertising business model change about tracking?

options.text: The advertisers become the customers, and users' interests come second
Advertising funding reduces the amount of tracking needed
Advertising funding has no effect on tracking either way
Advertising funding makes the users into the real customers

questions.explanation: Now the relationship between the company and the user whose data is being collected starts looking quite different: the user is given a free service and is coaxed into engaging with it as much as possible, and the tracking of the user serves not primarily that individual but rather the needs of the advertisers who are funding the service. The author thinks this relationship can be appropriately described with a word that has more sinister connotations: surveillance.

questions.question: Which thought experiment exposes what data collection really is, and how strong is the rhetoric?

options.text: Substituting 'surveillance' for 'data' in the usual phrases
Replace surveillance with data, which makes the phrases sound worse
It is offered as a neutral, non-judgmental observation
Substituting 'analytics' for 'tracking', presented as a neutral relabeling

questions.explanation: The joke title for the book itself is part of the self-labelling. In our attempts to make software 'eat the world' we have built the greatest mass surveillance infrastructure the world has ever seen: rushing toward an Internet of Things, we are rapidly approaching a world in which every inhabited space contains at least one internet-connected microphone, in the form of smartphones, smart TVs, voice-controlled assistant devices, baby monitors, and even children's toys that use cloud-based speech recognition — and many of these devices have a terrible security record.

questions.question: How does corporate data collection compare with what repressive regimes could achieve?

options.text: That totalitarian regimes could only dream of this reach
Modern surveillance is far less extensive than historical state surveillance
Corporate surveillance is fundamentally different in kind
Repressive regimes are not mentioned anywhere in the comparison

questions.explanation: Why are we seemingly happy to accept surveillance by corporations? Perhaps you feel you have nothing to hide — in other words, you are totally in line with existing power structures, you are not a marginalized minority, and you needn't fear persecution. Not everyone is so fortunate. Or perhaps it's because the purpose seems benign — it's not overt coercion and conformance, but merely better recommendations and more personalized marketing. However, combined with the discussion of predictive analytics, that distinction seems less clear.

questions.question: When does surveillance stop looking benign?

options.text: Insurance premiums tied to tracking devices, and typing inferred from a watch
Surveillance of this kind remains entirely benign in every case
Only surveillance by governments is ever genuinely non-benign
Insurance is the one genuinely benign application of tracking

questions.explanation: Consequential decisions and intrusive inference are what break the benign framing.

questions.question: What is wrong with the consent argument? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Users have little knowledge of what data they are feeding into our databases, or how it is retained and processed — and most privacy policies do more to obscure than to illuminate. Without understanding what happens to their data, users cannot give any meaningful consent

Often, data from one user also says things about other people who are not users of the service and who have not agreed to any terms — for example the derived datasets discussed in this book are precisely the kind of data where such implications arise

Data is extracted from users through a one-way process, not a relationship with true reciprocity, and not a fair value exchange: there is no dialog, no option for users to negotiate how much data they provide and what service they receive in return — the relationship between the service and the user is very asymmetric and one-sided, with the terms set by the service, not by the user
Consent forms of this kind turn out to be legally invalid in most jurisdictions anyway

questions.explanation: Three objections: knowledge, third parties, and asymmetry. Undoubtedly, social networks, search engines, and various other free online services are valuable to users — but there are problems with the consent argument.

questions.question: Why is 'just don't use it' not a free choice?

options.text: That opting out is not free when a service is effectively mandatory
It is a free choice, since no online service is truly essential
Declining is impossible in practice, since these services cannot be refused at all
Opting out is costless once you have read the privacy policy

questions.explanation: Declining to use a service due to its tracking of users is only an option for the small number of people who are privileged enough to have the time and knowledge to understand its privacy policy, and who can afford to potentially miss out on social participation or professional opportunities that may have arisen if they had participated. For people in a less privileged position there is no meaningful freedom of choice: surveillance becomes inescapable.

questions.question: Is privacy dead, and what does privacy actually mean?

options.text: That privacy means choosing what to reveal, not keeping everything secret
The claim is correct, and privacy really is dead
Privacy means keeping absolutely everything about yourself secret
Privacy is a property of the data rather than of the person

questions.explanation: When data is extracted from people through surveillance infrastructure, privacy rights are not necessarily eroded, but rather transferred to the data collector: companies that acquire data essentially say 'trust us to do the right thing with your data', which means that the right to decide what to reveal and what to keep secret is transferred from the individual to the company.

questions.question: Why do companies keep the outcome of surveillance secret?

options.text: Because it would seem creepy and would damage their business model
Because legal requirements forbid them from revealing it
Because the inferred data turns out to be worthless
They do not keep it secret; they publish it openly

questions.explanation: Even if particular users cannot be personally reidentified from the bucket of people targeted by a particular ad, they have lost their agency about the disclosure of some intimate information, such as whether they suffer from some illness: it is not the user who decides what is revealed to whom on the basis of their personal preferences — it is the company that exercises the privacy right with the goal of maximizing its profit.

questions.question: What do privacy settings achieve, and what do they leave untouched?

options.text: They restrain other users, but the service itself keeps full access
Privacy settings restrict the service's own access to the data
Privacy settings have no effect on other users either
Privacy settings fully solve the problem

questions.explanation: Many companies have a goal of not being perceived as creepy — avoiding the question of how intrusive their data collection actually is, and instead focusing on managing user perceptions. And even these perceptions are often managed poorly: for example, something may be factually correct, but if it triggers painful memories, the user may not want to be reminded about it. With any kind of data we should expect the possibility that it is wrong, undesirable, or inappropriate in some way, and we need to build mechanisms for handling those failures — whether something is 'undesirable' or 'inappropriate' is of course down to human judgment, and algorithms are oblivious to such notions unless we explicitly program them to respect human needs. As engineers of these systems we must be humble, accepting and planning for such failings.

questions.question: Why is this transfer of privacy rights unprecedented?

options.text: Because surveillance used to be expensive and manual, and trust was governed
Because surveillance is itself an entirely new phenomenon in human affairs
Because trust relationships are an entirely new phenomenon in human affairs
The situation is not in fact unprecedented in any respect worth noting

questions.explanation: Two dimensions of novelty: cost and scale, and absence of governance.

questions.question: What does the term 'data exhaust' suggest, and what is the correct view?

options.text: That behavioural data is worthless waste — whereas it is the core asset
The term is accurate, and behavioural data really is waste
The term refers to the network traffic overhead of tracking
It refers to the energy consumed by the datacenters storing it

questions.explanation: The inversion changes what the application is for. Two pieces of evidence that personal data really is a core asset: data brokers, a shady industry operating in secrecy, purchasing, aggregating, analyzing, inferring and reselling intrusive personal data about people, mostly for marketing purposes; and startup valuations, where startups are valued by their user numbers, by 'eyeballs' — that is, by their surveillance capabilities.

questions.question: Beyond the collecting company, who else wants the data and how might it escape? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Governments want to obtain it too, by means of secret deals, coercion, legal compulsion, or simply stealing it
When a company goes bankrupt, the personal data it has collected is one of the assets that get sold
Data is difficult to secure, so breaches happen disconcertingly often
Nobody else actually wants the data, and it never escapes the collecting company

questions.explanation: These observations have led critics to say that data is not just an asset, but a 'toxic asset', or at least 'hazardous material': even if we think we are capable of preventing abuse of data, whenever we collect data we need to balance the benefits with the risk of it falling into the wrong hands — computer systems may be compromised by criminals or hostile foreign intelligence services, data may be leaked by insiders, the company may fall into the hands of unscrupulous management that does not share our values, or the country may be taken over by a regime that has no qualms about compelling us to hand over the data.

questions.question: Against what time horizon must data collection decisions be judged?

options.text: Every possible future government, not just today's
Only the current legal and political environment
Only the coming financial year's requirements
No particular time horizon is relevant to making the decision

questions.explanation: Irreversibility is the underlying concern. 'Knowledge is power,' as the old adage goes — and furthermore, to scrutinize others while avoiding scrutiny oneself is one of the most important forms of power. This is why totalitarian governments want surveillance: it gives them the power to control the population. Although today's technology companies are not overtly seeking political power, the data and knowledge they have accumulated nevertheless gives them a lot of power over our lives, much of it surreptitious, outside of public oversight.

questions.question: Why is the Industrial Revolution the right comparison?

options.text: Because data is the defining feature of the information age
Because both of them were driven by the steam engine
Because both of them were purely beneficial in outcome
Because both of them were purely harmful in outcome

questions.explanation: It took a long time before safeguards were established — environmental protection regulations, safety protocols for workplaces, outlawing child labor and health inspections for food. Undoubtedly the cost of doing business increased when factories could no longer dump their waste into rivers, sell tainted foods, or exploit workers — but society as a whole benefited hugely, and few of us would want to return to a time before those regulations.

questions.question: Bruce Schneier compares data to something from an earlier industrial era. To what, and what follows for engineers?

options.text: To pollution: it festers like industrial waste, and our heirs will judge us
To capital: it is a pure asset with no downside, so collect all you can
To oil: a scarce extractable resource that engineers should refine
To electricity: a utility that should simply be metered and billed

questions.explanation: 'We should try to make them proud' is the sentence the chapter adds.

questions.question: The 1995 European Data Protection Directive places two requirements on personal data. Which, and how do they contradict Big Data practice?

options.text: Specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and not excessive
The Directive positively endorses maximal data collection
The Directive imposes no purpose limitation at all
The two positions turn out not to contradict one another

questions.explanation: The parenthetical doubt about consent is a callback to the earlier argument that users cannot give any meaningful consent. Updated regulations are now being developed.

questions.question: What three changes does the tech industry need in how it handles personal data?

options.text: Stop treating users as metrics, self-regulate, and educate them
Optimize metrics harder, lobby against regulation, and simplify policies
Wait for legislation, and change nothing voluntarily before then
Collect more data but anonymize it, and leave policy to lawmakers

questions.explanation: A culture shift in the tech industry with regard to personal data.

questions.question: Privacy is likened to a natural environment that needs active protection. Which claim does that analogy make?

options.text: Unprotected by legislation and cultural norms, privacy will be destroyed
Privacy is a private garden that each individual alone can protect
Ubiquitous surveillance is inevitable, and we must simply adapt
Privacy protects itself, since users abandon invasive services

questions.explanation: How exactly we might achieve this is an open question. To begin with, we should not retain data forever, but purge it as soon as it is no longer needed — purging data runs counter to the idea of immutability, but that issue can be solved. A promising approach is to enforce access control through cryptographic protocols, rather than merely by policy. Overall, culture and attitude changes will be necessary.

questions.question: Which claims about regulation hold? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: That it is doubtful whether the 1995 Directive is effective in today's internet context
That we should self-regulate our data collection and processing practices, in addition to noting that updated regulations are now being developed
That purging data runs counter to the idea of immutability, but that issue can be solved
That ubiquitous surveillance is inevitable and simply has to be accepted now

questions.explanation: The chapter explicitly says ubiquitous surveillance is not inevitable — we are still able to stop it. It also notes that to some extent industry opposition to regulation is justified, rather than dismissing it as entirely self-serving.

questions.question: You are about to add indefinite behavioral event tracking to a consumer app. On data-ethics grounds, what should change? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Retention: do not retain data forever, but purge it as soon as it is no longer needed, rather than keeping everything in case it turns out to be useful
Purpose: data should be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a way incompatible with those purposes

Consent: users have little knowledge of what data they are feeding into our databases, and most privacy policies do more to obscure than to illuminate — so take it upon yourself to educate end users about how their data is used, rather than keeping them in the dark
Scale: collect as much as you possibly can now, since storage is cheap and the data may prove useful later

questions.explanation: Collect-everything-in-case is the framing the chapter rejects. A fourth change it does prescribe: mechanism over policy — enforce access control through cryptographic protocols, for example that only the recommendations team may query this data, rather than merely by policy.

questions.question: Access control over personal data can rest on policy or on mechanism. Which is preferable, and how is it enforced?

options.text: Mechanism: enforce access through cryptographic protocols, not policy alone
Policy: a clearly written, published privacy policy is the strongest control
Obscurity: keep the schema undocumented so outsiders cannot write queries
Neither: access control conflicts with immutability and has to be dropped

questions.explanation: Enforcing access control cryptographically — so that, say, only the recommendations team can actually query a behavioral dataset — is stronger than a promise in a policy document. Purging data runs counter to the idea of immutability, but that issue can be solved; overall, culture and attitude changes will be necessary too.

questions.question: What do the evolution and recovery benefits of expressing dataflows as transformations amount to?

options.text: Rerun the new transformation code over the whole input
You can only add new steps, never change existing ones
Recovery requires restoring from backup
Expressing dataflows this way brings no evolution benefit at all

questions.explanation: These processes are quite similar to what databases already do internally, so the chapter recast the idea of dataflow applications as unbundling the components of a database, and building an application by composing these loosely coupled components. Derived state can be updated by observing changes in the underlying data, and moreover the derived state itself can further be observed by downstream consumers — we can even take this dataflow all the way through to the end-user device that is displaying the data, and thus build user interfaces that dynamically update to reflect data changes and continue to work offline.

questions.question: How can strong integrity guarantees be achieved scalably without distributed transactions?

options.text: End-to-end operation IDs plus asynchronous constraint checking
That only distributed transactions can provide integrity
That integrity must be sacrificed for scale
That clients must always wait for the constraint check

questions.explanation: By structuring applications around dataflow and checking constraints asynchronously, we can avoid most coordination and create systems that maintain integrity but still perform well, even in geographically distributed scenarios and in the presence of faults. We can then use audits to verify the integrity of data and detect corruption. Note the careful wording: avoid most coordination, not all.

questions.question: Which harms follow from data collection and use? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Making justifying decisions that seriously affect people's lives, and are difficult to appeal against
Leading to discrimination and exploitation
Normalizing surveillance and exposing intimate information
Higher infrastructure costs and slower software for users

questions.explanation: Cost and latency are not among them; the remaining harms it names are data breaches, and well-intentioned uses of data having unintended consequences — six harms in one sentence. The chapter — and the body of the book — ends: as software and data are having such a large impact on the world, we engineers must remember that we carry a responsibility to work toward the kind of world that we want to live in: a world that treats people with humanity and respect. 'I hope that we can work together toward that goal.'

questions.question: Compress the whole derived-data programme into its single argument.

options.text: Derive everything from a system of record, asynchronously, and verify it
Use a single distributed database with serializable transactions everywhere
Abandon derived data in favour of synchronous updates
Optimize for performance above correctness and ethics

questions.explanation: Derived data plus end-to-end correctness plus verification plus responsibility. Using only what this chapter says, the book has been for three things: that there is no universal tool, since there is no one single tool that can efficiently serve all possible use cases; that the hard problems are the distributed ones and they have known shapes, so you cannot just use a distributed transaction; and that derived data is the unifying idea — all in service of a world that treats people with humanity and respect.
